newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right gets voter message, left gloats.
newsitem.headline: French right gets voter message, left gloats.

text.p: French rightist politicians, reeling from a first-round parliamentary election setback, said they had registered voters' message of discontent as leftists gloated that power was within their grasp.

At the same time, mainstream candidates on the right and left bemoaned Sunday's record score of more than 15 percent for the extreme-right National Front and other fringe parties, which they said showed voters' frustration with the status quo.
"The French people meant above all to say that they wanted a real change, deep change. And we must listen to this message," conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe said.

French voters sent a message of warning to the governing centre-right majority and conservative President Jacques Chirac on Sunday by giving the left a substantial lead in the first round of the National Assembly election.

The vote put the left within reach of a stunning upset in next Sunday's runoff, according to voter surveys which suggested that France could be heading into a period of power-sharing between a left-wing government and a conservative president.

"I call on all those who want a more balanced government and a new policy for France to unite on this second round. All those who aspire to change must unite because a change of majority is possible and desirable," said Lionel Jospin, head of the opposition Socialist Party.

In his speech, Jospin said the Front's score was "high, too high" but offered its voters an olive branch, saying: "The next government must tackle as a priority the concerns of these French people who are worried and who believe themselves forgotten and threatened, so as to answer their expectations."
National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen called the result a major victory for his voters and a defeat for Chirac, and he called on the president to resign.
"President Chirac injected himself personally into the battle. He is defeated, he must leave," Le Pen told supporters.

It was Chirac who had dissolved parliament and called elections nearly 10 months ahead of schedule, seeking to ensure himself a friendly National Assembly for the final five years of his seven-year term.

Voter surveys said the Front, a xenophobic party which backs a constitutional preference for "native-born French people" in jobs and state benefits, might win up to three seats in the assembly, where it currently has none.
Le Pen urged Front voters to mobilise massively for next Sunday's run-off "so that the National Front can elect enough deputies to enable the voice of France to be heard".
Analysts speculated the vote could push Chirac into dumping Juppe, though centre-right leaders and cabinet members refrained from openly suggesting this on Sunday evening.

"As to changing the team, this is a matter for the president alone," Philippe Seguin, the outgoing National Assembly speaker, said in one of the few public, albeit vague, comments on Juppe's future status to come from a member of the government majority.
France's ecologists joined leftists in celebrating a surprisingly strong showing.
"You are looking at a happy man, this is an historic phenomenon. More than 20 Greens candidates will be present in the second round," said Greens' leader Jean-Luc Bennahmias.
He urged leftist voters to support any leftist candidate standing in the runoff, whether Socialist, Communist or ecologist.
